lesson.title: A second job: the lathe, start to finish

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the Zs bar cross the 0.87 Ω line at 0.977 Ω while the heat bar still passes, when you swap the lathe’s cpc from 2.5 mm² to 1.5 mm² at 27 m.
interactive.title: Which check sets the smallest cpc?
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Thirteen screens, with Back and Continue: a lathe motor's circuit designed end to end, whether its cpc can be smaller, and steel armour as the cpc.

Screen 1, Do you still have it? The question: “A motor circuit runs 27 m in 4 mm² singles with a 4 mm² cpc. Zs is 0.4 Ω at its board and 0.719 Ω at the motor. The client wants the cpc cut to 2.5 mm². Which checks must you work again?” Three choices, in this order: “Only the heat check”; “Zs against the breaker's maximum, and the heat check”; “The current rating and the voltage drop”. Right: “Still there.” Then the working. R1+R2 becomes 12.02 × 1.28 × 27 ÷ 1000 = 0.415 Ω. So Zs rises from 0.719 Ω to 0.815 Ω, which must stay within the breaker's maximum. The thinner cpc must still take the fault's heat. The cpc carries no load current, so the rating and the drop stay as they were. Then two buttons: Refresh the why (screen 2) and Skip to the practice (screen 5). Wrong, the first: “A thinner cpc has more resistance, so Zs rises too. Check it against the breaker's maximum.” Wrong, the third: “The cpc carries no load current, so neither changes. Its size changes Zs and the heat it can take.” Then the right working, and on to screen 2.

Screen 2, What it is for. “One whole job in one pass, on a circuit unlike the showroom's. A lathe motor is fed from a board that sits below 400 V. Its cable shares trunking with two other circuits. Then a question every designer meets. Can the cpc be smaller than Table 54.7's size? Yes, if two checks still pass. Zs must stay within the breaker's maximum. And the cpc must take the fault's heat.” In red, headed “If Zs is not rechecked”: “Cut the cpc on the heat check alone and Zs can rise past the maximum. Then the breaker may not open in time.”

Screen 3, The why: which check sets the smallest cpc. The picture: the lathe circuit from DB2, a line conductor and a cpc running to the motor, with the loop drawn as two parts: Zs at DB2, a fixed 0.4 Ω, and the circuit's R1+R2, which grows with the run and with a thinner cpc. A choice of cpc: 1.5, 2.5 or 4 mm², opening on 4 mm². A slider, run length, 10 to 40 m in steps of 0.5 m, opening on 27 m. Two bars. The first is Zs, built from the 0.4 Ω and the R1+R2, against a dashed line at 0.87 Ω, the maximum for the 25 A type C breaker.[^1] Past the line it turns red. The second is the least cpc the heat needs, against a mark at the cpc fitted. Two readouts. The first is the Cmin fault current, to 2 places, against 250 A. The second is the longest run this cpc allows, to 1 place. The rule beside it: “Zs = 0.4 + mΩ/m × 1.28 × length ÷ 1000. It must stay within 0.87 Ω. Least cpc = √(I² × 0.1) ÷ 143, with I = 253 ÷ Zs, the fault current at Cmax.” The mΩ/m for the 4 mm² line with each cpc: 16.71 with 1.5 mm², 12.02 with 2.5 mm², 9.22 with 4 mm². Below 250 A at Cmax, the breaker may not open within 0.1 s. Then the heat bar turns grey and reads “Heat: not worked here. The breaker may take longer than 0.1 s.” Below 250 A at Cmin, the Cmin readout turns red.

What he sees, at 27 m. 4 mm²: Zs 0.719 Ω, heat needs 0.78 mm². 2.5 mm²: R1+R2 0.415 Ω, Zs 0.815 Ω, heat needs 0.69 mm². 1.5 mm²: Zs 0.977 Ω, over the line. That gives 223.64 A at Cmin, under 250 A. Yet the heat needs only 0.57 mm². The words under it: “A thinner cpc raises Zs. That eases the heat but tightens the loop. On the lathe the loop, not the heat, sets the smallest cpc.” The prompt above the picture: “Pick a thinner cpc, then drag the length.” Read: at 27 m the 2.5 mm² cpc gives Zs 0.815 Ω, within 0.87 Ω. It needs only 0.69 mm² for the heat. The 1.5 mm² cpc gives 0.977 Ω and fails on Zs. Still: 2.5 mm², 27 m.

Screen 4, Check. “Keep the 2.5 mm² cpc. The lathe moves, and the run becomes 32 m. Is the circuit still acceptable?” Choices: “Yes: the cpc needs only 0.63 mm² for the heat”; “Yes: R1+R2 is 0.492 Ω, within 0.87 Ω”; “No: Zs is 0.892 Ω, over 0.87 Ω”. Right, the third: “R1+R2 = 12.02 × 1.28 × 32 ÷ 1000 = 0.492 Ω. Zs = 0.4 + 0.492 = 0.892 Ω, over 0.87 Ω. The longest run with 2.5 mm² is 30.5 m. Go back to the 4 mm² cpc, good to 39.8 m.” Wrong, the first: “The heat check does pass. But Zs is over the maximum, so the breaker may not open in time.” Wrong, the second: “Add Zs at DB2, 0.4 Ω. The breaker sees the whole loop.”

Screen 5, Worked example: steel armour as the cpc, a block at each press. The prompt: “Work each step yourself first, then press Show.” Said once: “Steel armour can be the cpc if it is big enough, by Table 54.7's ratio or by the adiabatic. Steel's k is far lower than copper's, so it needs more area.” The blocks:
A 6 mm² four-core 90 °C SWA. Table 54.7 asks for k1 ÷ k2 × S of armour. Take k1 = 143 for the copper and k2 = 46 for the steel. 46 is a practice value. On a real job, check it in Table 54.4. Armour needed = 143 × 6 ÷ 46 = 18.65 mm². The cable has 36 mm² of armour. Enough.
A 25 mm² four-core. Above 16 mm², up to 35 mm², Table 54.7 uses 16 in place of S.[^2] Armour needed = 143 × 16 ÷ 46 = 49.74 mm². The cable has 70 mm². Enough. Take armour areas from the maker's sheet for the cable you buy.
If it had fallen short, choose a cable with an extra core, or run a separate cpc alongside. A separate cpc must be sized for the whole fault current.
A 25 mm² five-core, 26 m, on a 40 A BS 88-2 fuse. Take Ze as 0.06 Ω. The fifth core and the armour share the cpc's job. Take 1.28 on the armour too. It runs cooler, so this errs safe. R2 = 1 ÷ (1 ÷ 0.727 + 1 ÷ 1.8) = 0.518 mΩ/m. R1+R2 = (0.727 + 0.518) × 1.28 × 26 ÷ 1000 = 0.041 Ω. Zs = 0.06 + 0.041 = 0.101 Ω. Fault current at Cmax = 253 ÷ 0.101 = 2504.95 A.
Work the heat at Cmax. It gives the larger area. Take 0.1 s for the fuse here, as a practice value. On a real job, read the time from Figure 3A3. Armour alone: √(2504.95² × 0.1) ÷ 46 = 17.22 mm², within its 88 mm². Core alone: √(2504.95² × 0.1) ÷ 143 = 5.54 mm², within 25 mm². Both pass.
Read: both four-core cables have more armour than Table 54.7 asks. With the core and the armour in parallel, Zs is 0.101 Ω. Each path alone takes the heat.

Screen 6, Section A, question 5 (a). The scenario panel, titled “The lathe at DB2”, in place of the showroom: “A workshop on a 400 V three-phase TN-C-S supply, Ze 0.12 Ω, prospective fault current 8 kA at the origin. DB2 is fed by a distribution circuit that drops 3%. Zs at DB2 is 0.4 Ω. From DB2, a circuit feeds a 12.5 kW three-phase lathe motor, power factor 0.91 and efficiency 94% at full load. It runs 27 m in 90 °C thermosetting singles in trunking on a wall, with two other loaded circuits, at 25 °C. Protection is a type C circuit-breaker to BS EN 60898.” Said once: “Use 0.4 Ω for Zs at DB2, even if you have 0.97 Ω written down. At 0.97 Ω no 25 A type C could pass.” The question: “(a) Determine the design current of the lathe circuit.” A typed answer, part 5a. U at DB2 = 400 × 0.97 = 388 V. √3 × 388 = 672.04. × 0.91 = 611.56. × 0.94 = 574.87. Ib = 12 500 ÷ 574.87 = 21.74 A. Accepted too: 21.7 A, and 21.77 A with √3 taken as 1.73. Slips: 21.09 A, “That is at 400 V. DB2 sits 3% down, at 388 V.” 20.44 A, “Divide by the efficiency too. The motor draws more than its output.” 19.79 A, “Divide by the power factor too.” 37.66 A, “It is three-phase: divide by √3 as well.” After two misses, the working.

Screen 7, Section A, question 5 (b) and (c). Part 5(a) carried forward. Shown as working: “(b) The next standard rating above 21.74 A is 25 A, type C.” Said once: “Assume the lathe's terminals and the breaker allow the cable to run at 90 °C. Table 4B1 gives Ca 1.02 for 90 °C thermosetting cable at 25 °C. It is above 1 because the tables are set at 30 °C. A cooler room takes heat away faster. Table 4C1 gives Cg 0.70 for three circuits in the trunking.” The question: “(c) Determine the minimum tabulated current-carrying capacity, It.” A typed answer, part 5c, to two places. Factors together = 1.02 × 0.70 = 0.714. It = 25 ÷ 0.714 = 35.01 A. Slips: 35.71 A, “Divide by Ca too. At 1.02 it lowers It a little.” 24.51 A, “Divide by Cg too. Three circuits share the trunking.” 30.45 A, “Work It from In, 25 A, not Ib.” After two misses, the working. Then (d): “In Table 4E1A, column 5, for three loaded singles, 2.5 mm² gives 28 A. That is too small. 4 mm² gives 37 A. Iz = 37 × 0.714 = 26.42 A, at least 25 A. So 4 mm².”

Screen 8, Section A, question 5 (e). Parts 5(a) to 5(d) carried forward. Said once: “Table 4E1B gives 10 mV/A/m for 4 mm², three-phase.” The question: “(e) Determine the voltage drop from the intake to the lathe, and state whether it complies.” A typed answer, part 5e, to two places. Upstream = 400 × 0.03 = 12.00 V. The lathe circuit, at 10 mV/A/m for 4 mm² three-phase: 10 × 21.74 × 27 ÷ 1000 = 5.87 V. Total = 12.00 + 5.87 = 17.87 V. Accepted too: 17.86 V from 21.7 A, and 17.88 V from 21.77 A. Slips: 5.87 V, “That is the lathe circuit alone. Add DB2's 3%, 12.00 V.” 12.80 V, “The whole path is three-phase, so add the 12.00 V as it is.” After two misses, the working. Then: “The limit for a power circuit is 5% of 400 V, 20.00 V, so it complies.”

Screen 9, Section A, question 5 (f) and (g). Parts 5(a) to 5(e) carried forward. Shown first: “(f) Table 54.7: a copper cpc with a line of 16 mm² or less is the line's size, so 4 mm².” Said once: “The client asks for a 2.5 mm² cpc to save copper. Table I1 gives 12.02 mΩ/m for a 4 mm² line with a 2.5 mm² cpc. Table I3 gives 1.28 to bring it up to 90 °C.” The question: “(g) Determine Zs at the lathe with a 2.5 mm² cpc, and state whether the circuit meets the requirements for automatic disconnection.” A typed answer, part 5g. R1+R2 = 12.02 × 1.28 × 27 ÷ 1000 = 0.415 Ω. Zs = 0.4 + 0.415 = 0.815 Ω. Accepted too: 0.82 Ω, rounded to two places, and 0.81 Ω, cut short, each with a note saying so. Slips: 0.725 Ω, “Multiply by 1.28 to take the cable up to its running temperature.” 0.535 Ω, “Start from Zs at DB2, 0.4 Ω, not Ze at the origin.” 0.719 Ω, “That is with the 4 mm² cpc. Use 12.02 mΩ/m, for 4 mm² with 2.5 mm².” After two misses, the working. Then: “0.815 Ω is within 0.87 Ω. At Cmin, 218.5 ÷ 0.815 = 268.10 A. That is past the 250 A that opens the breaker within 0.1 s. So it complies.”

Screen 10, Section A, question 5 (h). Parts 5(a) to 5(g) carried forward. Said once: “Table 54.3 gives k 143 for a copper cpc bunched with 90 °C thermosetting cables.” The question: “(h) Determine the minimum csa of the cpc for thermal constraints, and state whether 2.5 mm² is adequate.” A typed answer, part 5h, to two places. Fault current at Cmax = 230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.815 = 310.43 A. That is past 250 A, so the breaker opens within 0.1 s. Take t = 0.1 s. k = 143 for a copper cpc bunched with 90 °C thermosetting cables. S = √(310.43² × 0.1) ÷ 143 = 0.69 mm². Slips: 0.59 mm², “Work the heat at Cmax, 310.43 A. It gives the larger area.” 1.37 mm², “The breaker opens within 0.1 s at this current. 0.4 s is the limit, not the time.” 0.85 mm², “115 is for 70 °C thermoplastic. These cables are 90 °C thermosetting, so 143.” After two misses, the working. Then: “0.69 mm² is well under 2.5 mm², so it is adequate. Both checks pass. The loop is the closer one, at 0.815 Ω against 0.87 Ω.”

Screen 11, Section B: “The client asks for the lathe's cpc to be cut to 2.5 mm² to save copper. Explain whether you would agree, and what the inspector must be told.” Written, marked against three points, all of which make a full answer. One more go, then the model answer.

Screen 12, Section A, changed numbers. “A 40 A BS 88-2 fuse-switch feeds a 63 A TP&N workshop board through a 26 m distribution circuit. After diversity it carries 32 A per phase. It is 70 °C thermoplastic singles in trunking with two other circuits, at 35 °C. The drop must not exceed 6 V. Table 4B1 gives Ca 0.94 at 35 °C. Table 4C1 gives Cg 0.70 for three circuits. Determine the minimum tabulated current-carrying capacity, It.” A typed answer, in A, to two places. Ca = 0.94 at 35 °C, Cg = 0.70. Factors together = 0.94 × 0.70 = 0.658. It = 40 ÷ 0.658 = 60.79 A. Slips: 42.55 A, “Divide by Cg too.” 57.14 A, “Divide by Ca too.” 48.63 A, “Work It from In, 40 A, not the 32 A load.” After it: “In Table 4D1A, column 5, 10 mm² gives 50 A. That is too small, so 16 mm² at 68 A. Its drop is 2.4 × 32 × 26 ÷ 1000 = 2.00 V, inside 6 V. The board's 63 A rating is at least the 40 A fuse ahead of it, as Regulation 536.4.202 asks.[^3]”

Screen 13, Keep this: the summary card, its figures headed “The lathe so far”, then Finish the lesson.

On every screen, each line is worked from the rounded figures shown before it. Each screen that uses a practice value says so.
interactive.ignores: The picture holds Zs at DB2 at 0.4 Ω and takes the whole run at 90 °C through the 1.28 multiplier. It takes the breaker to open within 0.1 s whenever the Cmax current reaches 250 A, and works the heat only then. It leaves out the motor’s starting current, parallel earth paths and DB2’s own fault level. The armour example puts the 1.28 multiplier on the steel too. That errs on the safe side, because armour runs cooler than the cores.

explain.text:
Table 54.7's cpc needs no calculation. For a copper line of 16 mm² or less, it is the line's own size. That is the suitable size, not the smallest.[^35] The smallest that works is the [[minimum cpc]], and only a calculation finds it. A thinner cpc saves copper, but it has more resistance. So R1+R2 rises, and Zs with it. Two checks must still pass.

The first is the loop. At 250 A the breaker opens within 0.1 s. At Cmin the supply can sag to 218.5 V. So the loop must stay under 218.5 ÷ 250 = 0.874 Ω. The table rounds it to 0.87 Ω. A bigger loop lets less than 250 A flow, and the breaker may not open in time. The second is the heat. The cpc must carry the fault until the breaker opens. Work it at the Cmax current.[^36]

The two checks pull opposite ways. A higher Zs lets less fault current flow. While the breaker still trips at once, less current heats the cpc less. So the heat check gets easier as the loop check gets harder. Once the current is too low for that, the breaker slows down. Then the heat climbs again. On the lathe, a 2.5 mm² cpc gives Zs 0.815 Ω and needs only 0.69 mm² for the heat. A 1.5 mm² cpc fails on Zs, at 0.977 Ω. Worked at the Cmax current, it would still pass the heat.

Steel armour can be the cpc when a calculation shows it is enough. Steel's k is far lower than copper's. The same fault heats it further, so it needs more area. Table 54.7 scales the line's size by k1 ÷ k2, the copper's k over the steel's. Above 16 mm², up to 35 mm², it uses 16 in place of the line's size.[^2] If the armour falls short, use a cable with an extra core, or run a separate cpc alongside. A separate cpc must be sized for the whole fault current.[^37] Where a core and the armour share the job, their resistances combine in parallel.

**Table 54.7's cpc needs no calculation. A smaller one passes only when Zs and the heat check both still hold. On the lathe, the loop runs out first.**

analogy.text: Think of a crane’s safe working load. Two limits set it: the rope’s strength and the jib’s tipping. Close in, the rope runs out first. Far out along the jib, tipping does. The cpc has two limits as well: the loop and the heat. On a short run with plenty of copper, neither bites. Lengthen the run or thin the cpc, and on the lathe the loop runs out first.
analogy.breaks: A crane’s limits are fixed by its maker and printed on a chart. A cpc’s limits move with the board’s Zs, the breaker and the run, so you work both for every circuit. And a lower fault current eases the heat only while the breaker still trips at once.

practice.text:
- Work Ib at the board's own voltage: U × (1 − the upstream drop).
- Choose the breaker: the next standard rating at or above Ib. Type C suits a motor's starting current.
- Find It = In ÷ (the factors that act together). Read the cable from the column for its method.
- Add every drop from the intake. Judge the total against 3% or 5% of the supply.
- Take Table 54.7's cpc. To go smaller, work Zs with the smaller cpc against the maximum, then the heat at the Cmax current.
- Work the longest run the cpc allows: (max Zs − Zs at the board) × 1000 ÷ (mΩ/m × multiplier).
- For armour as the cpc, use Table 54.7 with k1 ÷ k2, or the adiabatic with the steel's k. Take the armour's area and resistance from the maker's sheet for the cable you buy.
- Where a cpc passes by a small margin, hand the inspector the expected cold reading.

**Rule of thumb:** if the cpc is smaller than the line, work both checks, Zs first.

**Worked example:** the lathe at 27 m, 4 mm² line, 2.5 mm² cpc. R1+R2 = 12.02 × 1.28 × 27 ÷ 1000 = 0.415 Ω. Zs = 0.4 + 0.415 = 0.815 Ω, within 0.87 Ω. At Cmax, 253 ÷ 0.815 = 310.43 A. The heat needs √(310.43² × 0.1) ÷ 143 = 0.69 mm². Both pass, up to 30.5 m.

**Common mistakes**
- Checking only the heat when the cpc is cut.
- Working the heat at the Cmin current.
- Calling Table 54.7's size the minimum.
- Working Ib at 400 V when the board sits lower.
- Taking armour areas from another cable's figures. Use the maker's sheet for the cable bought.

b1.q: The client asks for the lathe’s cpc to be cut to 2.5 mm² to save copper. Explain whether you would agree, and what the inspector must be told.

points.text: Both checks pass. Zs at the lathe is 0.815 Ω, within the breaker’s 0.87 Ω maximum. So 268.10 A flows at Cmin and opens it within 0.1 s. The cpc needs only 0.69 mm² for the heat, so 2.5 mm² is enough.
points.cite: BS 7671 Table 41.3 (0.87 Ω, 25 A type C); Fig 3A5, Ia 250 A (mock 2 p.2); slides p.47 (Cmin); Slides p.58 to 62 (S = √(I²t) ÷ k, Cmax); Table 54.3, k 143 (mock 2 p.2)

points.text: The margin is thin. With 2.5 mm², the run can be no longer than 30.5 m, so a longer route or a later extension would fail. Table 54.7’s 4 mm² is the suitable size. A smaller cpc stands only on this calculation.
points.cite: OSG Table I1 p.218 (12.02 mΩ/m); OSG Table I3 p.220 (1.28); the longest-run rule, lesson 6; Course flowchart note 2; NICEIC/ELECSA, Table 54.7 as an alternative to calculation

points.text: Tested cold at 20 °C, it should read about 0.725 Ω. That is over the 0.680 Ω rule of thumb, 0.87 × 250 ÷ 320. Yet the circuit complies. Only the circuit warms up. Zs at DB2 does not. So hand the inspector the expected reading and the reason it passes.
points.cite: OSG p.139 and p.146 (Table B8, (t + 230) rule); Voltimum (cold reading 80% of tabulated); lesson 9

b1.model: It complies, but I would advise against it. With a 2.5 mm² cpc, Zs at the lathe is 0.815 Ω, within the breaker’s 0.87 Ω. So 268.10 A flows at Cmin and opens it within 0.1 s. For the heat the cpc needs only 0.69 mm², so 2.5 mm² is enough. But the margin is thin. The run can be no longer than 30.5 m. Table 54.7’s 4 mm² is the suitable size. A smaller cpc stands only on this calculation. So I would keep 4 mm². If 2.5 mm² goes in, I would tell the inspector to expect about 0.725 Ω cold. That is over the 0.680 Ω rule of thumb, yet it passes. Only the circuit warms up. Zs at DB2 does not.

summary.title: A second job: the lathe, start to finish
summary.for: One pass through a whole design. Work Ib at the board’s own voltage. Choose the device, then the cable for where it runs. Add every drop from the intake. Then choose the cpc. Table 54.7’s size needs no calculation. A smaller one is fine only when Zs and the heat check both pass.
summary.rule:
U at the board = U × (1 − the upstream drop)
It ≥ In ÷ (Ca × Cg). Ca is above 1 below 30 °C
Drop from the intake = upstream + mV/A/m × Ib × L ÷ 1000
Smaller cpc: Zs ≤ max Zs, and S ≥ √(I² × t) ÷ k at Cmax
Longest run = (max Zs − Zs at the board) × 1000 ÷ (mΩ/m × multiplier)
Armour: at least k1 ÷ k2 × S, with 16 for S above 16 mm², up to 35 mm²
Core and armour: R2 = 1 ÷ (1 ÷ Ra + 1 ÷ Rc)

Armour short? Use a cable with an extra core, or a separate cpc sized for the whole fault current.

traps.text: Checking only the heat when the cpc is cut. A thinner cpc raises Zs too.

Calling Table 54.7’s size the minimum. It is the suitable size. Only a calculation gives the minimum.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the Zs bar cross the 0.87 Ω line at 0.977 Ω while the heat bar still passes, when you swap the lathe’s cpc from 2.5 mm² to 1.5 mm² at 27 m.

warnings: The page height keeps growing with the frame (avoid vh units and height:100%). [at 340 and 1040 px wide]

applied.problem: Table 54.7 uses 16 in place of S only for 16 < S ≤ 35 mm² (above 35 mm² it uses S/2), so "above 16 mm²" overreaches its quote; the 1.5 mm² heat pass holds only worked at Cmax, since 223.64 A at Cmin may not trip it in 0.1 s; "trips at once" is "within 0.1 s".
The armour line says 16 replaces S for every line above 16 mm²; Table 54.7 does that only up to 35 mm² (its cited row is 16 < S ≤ 35), and uses S/2 above that.

Screen 5 says Table 54.7 uses 16 for any S above 16 mm², but only for 16 < S ≤ 35 mm²; and "Cmax gives the larger area" holds there only because t is fixed at 0.1 s: for a fuse, a lower current can take longer and give a larger I²t.

"Cmax gives the larger area" is stated generally; it holds while the device opens within the same 0.1 s, but for a fuse or a breaker in its slower region a lower current can take longer and need a larger area.

notes.problem: Ze 0.12 Ω, the 8 kA prospective fault current and the 27 m run are marked constant with no source, though mock 1 p.1 states all three; sources are frozen, so recorded only.
Screen 12 cites Regulation 536.4.202 from a guide to Amendment 4, while his copy is BS 7671:2018+A2:2022; worth confirming the regulation and wording in the edition he works to.

Screen 12 follows the shape of C&G 2396-402 (Dec 2014) Section A and keeps its 35 °C ambient and 70 °C thermoplastic singles in trunking; all other figures differ, so not a copy, but the ambient could be changed on a rebuild.

Screen 3 and the screen 4 slip say the 1.5 mm² (and 32 m) cpc passes the heat; true only as the model works it (t = 0.1 s at the Cmax current); at Cmin the breaker may not open in 0.1 s. The ignores panel discloses this; kept as is.
